keyVerseText: And the sons of Pedaiah were, Zerubbabel, and Shimei: and the sons of Zerubbabel; Meshullam, and Hananiah, and Shelomith their sister:
rootMeaning: The name זְרֻבָּבֶל (Zerubbabel) derives from the Hebrew root זָרַב (zârab), which means to wax warm or to flow away, combined with the term בָּבֶל (Babylon). Thus, Zerubbabel literally means "sown in Babylon" or "descended from Babylon," reflecting one who was born or begotten in Babylon. This etymology conveys a sense of origin and planting, suggesting a new beginning or growth emerging from exile and foreign soil, which enriches the understanding beyond the simple proper name.
usageInScripture: The name Zerubbabel appears 21 times in Scripture, consistently referring to the same historical individual—an Israelite leader and grandson of King Jehoiachin. Translations frequently render the name simply as "Zerubbabel" or in phrases such as "of Zerubbabel" or "with Zerubbabel," indicating his prominent role in the restoration community. The repeated association with leadership and return from Babylonian exile underscores his significance as a key figure in Israel’s post-exilic history.
theologicalSignificance: Zerubbabel’s name, meaning "sown in Babylon," highlights God’s providential work through exile and restoration. Though born in captivity, Zerubbabel became a leader of the returning exiles, demonstrating that God can raise up faithful servants even from places of judgment and displacement. This truth points forward to the redemptive work of Christ, who brings new life and restoration to a fallen people. Understanding Zerubbabel’s name reminds believers that God’s purposes prevail through apparent setbacks, and His plans for renewal are often rooted in places of brokenness.
keyVerseReflection: 1 Chronicles 3:19 names Zerubbabel as a son of Pedaiah and lists his children, emphasizing his place in the Davidic lineage. The use of Zerubbabel’s name here anchors him historically and genealogically, highlighting his role as a covenantal link between the monarchy and the post-exilic community. The meaning "sown in Babylon" enriches this verse by reminding readers that God’s promises endure through generations, even those born in exile, pointing to His faithfulness in preserving His chosen line.
